components.title: The Water Cycle
components.subtitle: How water moves between the oceans, the air, and the land

components.text: Heat from the Sun turns liquid water in oceans, lakes, and rivers into water vapour. Plants also release water vapour through tiny pores in their leaves. This plant process is called transpiration.
As water vapour rises, it cools. Cooler air holds less vapour, so the vapour turns back into liquid. It condenses onto tiny particles such as dust, forming droplets that gather into clouds.
When cloud droplets grow heavy enough, they fall as rain, snow, sleet, or hail. This water collects in oceans, lakes, rivers, and underground aquifers, and the cycle starts again.
Worked example: a puddle after rain

items.label: Sun warms the puddle
items.text: Sunlight heats the shallow water, so some molecules gain enough energy to escape as vapour (evaporation).

items.label: Vapour rises and cools
items.text: The vapour climbs into cooler air, where it condenses onto dust particles and forms a small cloud.

items.label: Droplets fall
items.text: The droplets merge until they are heavy enough to fall as light rain, returning water to the ground.

items.label: Water re-collects
items.text: The rain refills the puddle and soaks into the soil, so the cycle repeats.

questions.question: What process moves water from plant leaves into the air?
questions.explanation: Transpiration is the release of water vapour through the pores in plant leaves.

questions.question: Why does water vapour form clouds as it rises?
options: It is pushed down by wind
questions.explanation: Cooler air holds less vapour, so the vapour condenses into droplets around particles such as dust.

questions.question: Which of these is a form of precipitation?
questions.explanation: Snow, like rain, sleet, and hail, is water that falls from clouds.
